clue.text: Gamp discharged from hospital?

definitions.meaning: a gamp is a big umbrella, and one given new fabric has had its canopy replaced
a patient sent home from hospital is well again

explanation.surface: A Mrs Gamp-style nurse is sent home from the ward.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Gamp is the nurse in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit, whose umbrella gave 'gamp' its sense; the answer split RE-COVERED fits the umbrella, read whole it fits the patient.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as RE-COVERED it is an umbrella with a new canopy; read whole it describes a patient restored to health and sent home.

clue.text: Much sought after

parts.note: the French verb for 'seek' gives a word for 'rare, choice', which literally means sought with care

explanation.definitionFit: A choice, exquisite thing is one hunted out with effort, the literal sense of the French past participle.

clue.text: Tea from 9 without it

indicators.note: the clue's 9 has its two letters spelling 'it' taken away, and what remains is rearranged

parts.note: 9 points to the answer at 9 across, a Tuscan red wine

explanation.surface: A tea is brewed from a wine with something removed.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking I and T out of the 9-across wine leaves CHIAN, whose letters are rearranged; the clue gives no separate anagram signal, so 'without' does the work of a composite.
explanation.definitionFit: China tea is the type grown in China, so the country's name serves for the drink.

clue.text: Changed course about two points and put on a topcoat

indicators.note: the turning manoeuvre goes round the compass letters, so one piece sits around the other

parts.note: to veer is to change course
N and E are two points of the compass, north and east

explanation.surface: A sailor tacks and then pulls on a coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topcoat' suggests clothing, but here it is a thin decorative surface layer, such as fine wood laid over cheaper timber.
explanation.definitionFit: Veneering is covering a surface with a thin decorative outer layer.

clue.text: Platelayers' persiflage?

parts.note: platelayers lay railway lines, so their teasing banter would be named after the lines they handle

explanation.definitionFit: Persiflage is light mockery or banter, and the answer is good-humoured teasing whose first four letters are the platelayers' rails.

clue.text: Rose up before I have to descend

indicators.note: in a down entry the colour word is written upwards, so it reads backwards

parts.note: rose is a shade of red
've is the short form of have

explanation.surface: A rose climbed up before the speaker had to come down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like the past tense of rise, but it is the colour; in a down entry 'up' means written bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: To derive from a source is to descend or come from it, as words descend from older forms.

clue.text: Territorial division of horse

definitions.meaning: an English county is a territorial division
a large heavy draught horse breed of the English Midlands

explanation.definitionFit: A county is an English administrative area, and the same word names a breed of heavy draught horse.

clue.text: Sun-route to the Border?

parts.note: Sol is the Latin name for the sun
a way is a route

explanation.surface: Following the sun's path north to the frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: The Border is the England–Scotland boundary; the Solway Firth is the estuary along which it runs to the sea, so the question mark marks a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Solway Firth is the sea inlet marking the western end of the England–Scotland frontier.

clue.text: " The Greys " mechanized vehicle?

parts.note: the Scots Greys were a cavalry regiment on grey mounts; mechanize a grey mount and you have a metal one, the old name for a steam locomotive

explanation.definitionFit: A steam locomotive was nicknamed a metal steed, and an iron-grey coat is a horse colour.

clue.text: Would you let on, Reverend?

indicators.note: the question asks whether the letters will be let out of their order, prompting a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Asking a clergyman whether he will reveal a secret.
explanation.walkthrough: The Reverend Mr Elton is the vicar in Jane Austen's Emma; 'let on' is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The clergyman Mr Elton is a vicar in Jane Austen's novel Emma.

clue.text: Can I hit on a drink?

indicators.note: being 'on' the bottle means tipsy, so the letters reel into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone asks if they may hit the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' signals the anagram of CAN I HIT; 'a drink' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A red wine from Tuscany, served as a drink.

clue.text: Exclude as umpires may

definitions.meaning: to exclude is to dismiss a possibility
a cricket umpire gives a batsman out by ruling on an appeal

explanation.definitionFit: To dismiss a possibility, and literally what a cricket umpire does when giving a batsman out.

clue.text: To dispense with public relations leaves the bishop buoyant

indicators.note: dispensing with something means doing without it, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: a prelate is a senior churchman such as a bishop

explanation.surface: Sacking the PR team leaves a bishop in high spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To dispense with' removes PR from PRELATE; 'elate' as an adjective is an old form meaning in high spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Elate is an old adjective meaning in high spirits, just as buoyant does.

clue.text: He's a deep one, difficult to hook

definitions.text: He's a deep one, difficult to hook

parts.words: He's a deep one, difficult to hook
parts.note: the Book of Job asks whether the great sea monster can be drawn out with a hook

explanation.definitionFit: The biblical sea monster of Job 41 lives in the deep and cannot be caught with a fishhook.

clue.text: "The noble lord who rules the State, The noble lord who cleans the plate … They all shall equal be "?

definitions.text: "The noble lord who rules the State, The noble lord who cleans the plate … They all shall equal be "?

parts.words: "The noble lord who rules the State, The noble lord who cleans the plate … They all shall equal be "?
parts.note: the lines are from Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers, where lords and servants alike become equals, each a companion of the same rank

explanation.definitionFit: Compeers are equals or companions of the same standing, and the verse makes every noble lord the equal of the rest.

clue.text: They didn't get fired from the Ministry

definitions.text: They didn't get fired from the Ministry

parts.words: They didn't get fired from the Ministry
parts.note: 'fired' reads as dismissed from a government department, but means shot from guns; the Ministry was the First World War department of armaments

explanation.definitionFit: Shells and bullets are fired from guns, and Britain had a wartime department named after them.

clue.text: For-men?

parts.note: people who are in favour of something are those 'for' it, and the word is also short for professionals

explanation.definitionFit: Arguments or people in favour are the 'fors' in a debate, the Latin word for 'for' made plural.

clue.text: Spirited school of oratory?

parts.note: a place teaching people to talk freely, but 'spirited' points to illicit spirits sold in a Prohibition bar

explanation.definitionFit: A Prohibition-era illicit bar sold spirits, and its name split in two sounds like an instruction to talk freely.

clue.text: Panelled Scotch-cart

parts.note: a wain is a farm wagon or cart
a Scot is a Scotch person

explanation.surface: A carved wooden panel of a Scottish farm wagon.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in reverse of the clue's order: 'cart' gives WAIN first, then 'Scotch' gives SCOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Wainscot is wooden panelling on the lower part of a room's walls, used here as a verb of covering in panels.

clue.text: Cauliflower in box

parts.note: a boxer's ear swollen by punches is called a cauliflower ear, so 'box' is the sport, not a container

explanation.definitionFit: A swollen ear from being punched, as a boxer's cauliflower ear, or as a cuff round the head.

clue.text: Wings for the Navy in the East

annotationWithheld.why: Wings for the Navy in the East (4): ERNE needs RN with an E on each side, but 'the East' gives only one E and no other word supplies the second unless 'Wings' does two jobs as both definition (the sea eagle) and the outer letters
annotationWithheld.clue: Wings for the Navy in the East

clue.text: Fee simple in Wool?

parts.note: a fee is paid in cash
mere means simple or plain

explanation.surface: Legal jargon: a fee simple, an estate held outright, here held in wool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fee simple' is a legal term for absolute ownership of land, which disguises the two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is fine soft wool from Kashmir goats.

clue.text: Quietly to hint the complexion needs attention

parts.note: p, for piano, is the musical direction for quietly
to imply is to hint

explanation.surface: Gently suggesting someone's skin needs care.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotty skin with many blemishes is a complexion in need of treatment.

clue.text: One largely expectant but not shortly

definitions.text: One largely expectant but not shortly

parts.words: One largely expectant but not shortly
parts.note: the hero of Dickens's Great Expectations is known by a short three-letter name, but his full surname is longer

explanation.walkthrough: Pip in Great Expectations is Philip Pirrip in full: 'largely' asks for the long form, 'not shortly' rules out Pip.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip, hero of Dickens's Great Expectations, bears this full surname rather than his short nickname.

clue.text: For the train one cap from the top drawer

indicators.note: the letters are exchanged for others, standing in place of a rearrangement

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone buying a cap for a train journey from a high-class shop.
explanation.walkthrough: TRAIN, I and CAP are rearranged; 'top drawer' is the idiom for upper class.
explanation.definitionFit: Patrician means aristocratic, the upper-class sense of 'top drawer'.

clue.text: Write about the return of Bill, the Nut

indicators.note: the writing word goes around the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: to pen is to write

indicators.note: a return is a coming back, so the bill's letters are read backwards

parts.note: AC, short for account, is a bill

explanation.surface: Writing about a returned bill from a crank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' suggests an eccentric, but it is the edible kind; 'Bill' is an account, a common crossword shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: A pecan is a nut from a North American hickory tree.

clue.text: It comes up against the Education Board

definitions.text: It comes up against the Education Board

parts.words: It comes up against the Education Board
parts.note: the board is a classroom blackboard, and what a teacher writes with is pressed against it

explanation.definitionFit: Teachers write on a blackboard with sticks of soft white limestone.

clue.text: Very musical dolt dogged by sloth

indicators.note: to be dogged is to be followed, so the second piece comes after

parts.note: an ass is a fool or dolt
the ai is a three-toed sloth

explanation.surface: A fool is followed around by a lazy animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The ai is a three-toed sloth, a crossword favourite; the definition means 'very' as a musical direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Assai is the Italian musical direction for very, as in allegro assai.

clue.text: Flying hatchet

parts.note: the word for a small axe also names an aircraft with spinning rotor blades

explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a helicopter, which flies, and also a small axe or cleaver.

clue.text: Chinatown

parts.note: split as china and town: a London district famous for its eighteenth-century porcelain works

explanation.definitionFit: Chelsea porcelain was made in that London borough, so the place is both a china and a town.

clue.text: Retrospective article on bad housing — bad

indicators.note: looking back over the past, so the article's letters are read backwards

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
a sty is a filthy dwelling, a pigsty

explanation.surface: A newspaper looks back on poor housing conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrospective' turns AN into NA; 'article' looks like a newspaper piece but is the grammar word.
explanation.definitionFit: Nasty means unpleasant or bad.

clue.text: What a state to be in because a chap gets kidded!

definitions.text: What a state to be in because a chap gets kidded!

parts.words: What a state to be in because a chap gets kidded!
parts.note: 'kidded' looks like teased but means having had a kid, a child

explanation.definitionFit: Fatherhood is the condition a man enters on having a child.
